newsitem.title: INDIA: INTERVIEW-India must push privatisation - Coopers.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-India must push privatisation - Coopers.

text.p: India must back promises to continue its economic reforms programme with speedy action or risk alienating investors, officials from auditing and consultancy firm Coopers & Lybrand said on Tuesday.
"Quite frankly, there has been a great deal of talk but we are yet to see the action," said Peter Benson, chairman of Coopers & Lybrand's international privatisation division.
Benson is in the Indian capital to attend a conference on infrastructure organised by the U.N. Economic and Social Commission for Asia and the Pacific (ESCAP).
He said India was unlikely to achieve its fiscal 1996/97 (April-March) target of raising 50 billion rupees from a programme of partial privatisation of state-run companies.

"Privatisation needs a very strong lead from the top. In the U.K., Margaret Thatcher drove it through...she cut through the civil service. India needs that real political determination that will result in action," Benson said.
Adrian Howcroft, also of the firm's international privatisation division, said India should focus more on getting small core projects off the ground.
"There are an awful lot of very big, high-profile projects and the larger the project, the bigger the risk. India should complete lots of small projects and build on that," he said.
Benson said the biggest factor that discouraged investment in small projects across Asia was bureaucracy.
"In India too, investors are struggling through the undergrowth of bureaucracy," Benson said.
Another worrying factor, especially in countries like Vietnam and Burma, was political uncertainty, he said.
"Elsewhere, like in Thailand, it's the sheer scale of growth, where growth is increasing so fast it's almost unable to keep up with its own growth."
Benson said most investors had not yet come to grips with China but the size of its market made it difficult to ignore.
"All our major clients are in China because if the market opens up and they get left behind it could destroy them globally," Benson said.
"The private sector wants a fair return for a fair day's work commensurate with the risk. In China, the risk is higher than the reward," he said.
Howcroft said he saw a slight movement of investments away from China and into other Asian countries.

"There is a bit of a switch as multinationals are tired of battering their heads in China. Motor manufacturers are looking at this part of the world and some of that investment is bouncing back into India," he said.
He said Asian countries would have to be increasingly competitive to attract foreign funds.
"There's a lot of money available but only those countries that can make it easier for investors will get on the approval list," he said.
Howcroft said communication between state governments and the Indian federal government must be strengthened and there should be clear regulations governing foreign direct investment.
"India must get the system of regulation up and running before the process (of opening up) starts," he said.
